title: Epidemiology

jokes.text: George Takei narrating Halloween intro: 'A time of vampires, hobgoblins, Draculas, boogens and headless mice. I'm George Takei. You know what? Let's just get to it.'
jokes.setup: Dramatic, portentous Halloween narration listing spooky things — sounds like a serious horror intro
jokes.punchline: Takei abruptly abandons the bit mid-pretension ('You know what? Let's just get to it.'), undercutting the grandeur and acknowledging the audience's awareness of the gimmick
jokes.explanation: Smart cold open joke. The setup mimics every portentous Halloween special intro, then Takei's bored deflation ('You know what? Let's just get to it.') is a perfectly timed self-aware puncture. The word 'boogens' is an absurdist detail that signals the show's register immediately. Good economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: George Takei
dialogue.line: Boogens and headless mice? That's not a traditional Halloween creature list.

jokes.text: Dean dressed as Lady Gaga: 'Ah-ah-ah. Chef Gaga never reveals her caterer. And don't try reading my pa- pa- pa- poker face.'
jokes.setup: Someone asks how the dean got the food spread; Dean is dressed as Lady Gaga
jokes.punchline: Dean commits fully to the Lady Gaga bit, reworking 'Poker Face' lyrics as a deflection — 'Chef Gaga' and the stuttered 'pa-pa-pa-poker face' — while evading a legitimate question
jokes.explanation: Classic Dean Pelton character comedy — his obsessive commitment to a costume bit while avoiding real questions is perfectly in character. 'Chef Gaga' is a cute portmanteau. The sung stutter of 'pa-pa-pa-poker face' earns the laugh through dedication to the bit.

dialogue.speaker: George Takei
dialogue.line: I'm George Takei, and I'll be your narrator for this evening.

dialogue.speaker: George Takei
dialogue.line: Just kidding, I don't care about any of you.

jokes.text: Jeff immediately deflates the Dean's mystery: 'It's military rations from an Army surplus store.' Beat. 'I didn't read your poker face, you left the containers in the garbage.'
jokes.setup: Dean dramatically refuses to reveal the caterer, playing up the mystery
jokes.punchline: Jeff reveals the mundane truth instantly — not from cleverness but from laziness on the Dean's part — then anticipates and deflects the Dean's protest
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff deflation joke. The double structure — first revealing the truth, then preemptively rebutting the Dean's objection ('I didn't read your poker face, you left the containers in the garbage') — is tight and character-specific. Jeff's particular brand of effortless superiority makes this land.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: You want to know about the catering? Po-po-po-poker face, po-po-poker face.

jokes.text: Dean's iTunes exposed — voice memos include: 'Note to self: Get oil changed. Check Netflix for that movie where Greg Kinnear plays a ghost. No, an angel. And something called Human Centi...'
jokes.setup: Jeff tells the Dean his iTunes is also playing his personal voice memos when it's not on the ABBA loop
jokes.punchline: The memos escalate from mundane (oil change) to embarrassing (Greg Kinnear angel movie confusion) to cut off at 'Human Centi-' — implying Human Centipede, which is too shocking to complete
jokes.explanation: Genuinely excellent joke construction. Three-part escalation: mundane errand → confused film recollection (the Greg Kinnear 'ghost/angel' hedge is a great character detail) → cut off mid-word on 'Human Centi-' which the audience completes in horror. The incompleteness is funnier than any punchline could be. Character-specific for the Dean (obsessive about pop culture, oblivious to shame). The ABBA loop setup pays off perfectly when we learn *voice memos* are also leaking out.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: The catering arrangements are classified. Lady Gaga doesn't reveal her secrets.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It's just sandwiches, Dean.

jokes.text: ABBA's greatest hits / endless loop detail as part of the Dean's iTunes revelation
jokes.setup: Jeff reveals the Dean's iTunes has been playing at the party
jokes.punchline: It's on an endless loop of ABBA's greatest hits — perfectly in character for Dean Pelton's maximalist, theatrical sensibility
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat — ABBA suits the Dean's flamboyant persona — but it's the first part of the escalating joke rather than a standalone. Counts as its own comic beat in the setup of #4.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I know exactly where this catering came from. The napkins are from Señor Kevin's, the cups are from Boco Roco's, and the little toothpicks are from—

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: We just threw all the leftovers together.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: ...I was going to say Ming's.

jokes.text: Costume guessing: 'David Beckham. Dragon turtle? T. Rex.'
jokes.setup: Someone is wearing a costume and people try to guess what it is
jokes.punchline: The guesses are wildly off and escalate from plausible (Beckham) to absurd (dragon turtle) to prehistoric (T. Rex), suggesting the costume is genuinely ambiguous or bad
jokes.explanation: Functional running gag setup — the bad-costume guessing game — but the guesses themselves aren't particularly inspired. 'Dragon turtle' is the best of them. Sets up a recurring bit.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Dean, your iTunes is synced to the school's PA system.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: What? No, that's impossible.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Your entire playlist just played over every speaker in the building.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Oh my God, what was playing?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: 'Feelings' by Morris Albert on repeat. Followed by 'I'm Every Woman.'

jokes.text: Jeff to Troy (in elaborate cardboard robot costume): 'Man, I wonder how much effort you put into being accidentally handsome for a costume every year. Half the effort you'll be putting into eating and drinking.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is dressed as 'David Beckham' (or simply himself in a nice suit) while Troy has an elaborate handmade costume
jokes.punchline: Jeff acknowledges his own effortless handsomeness as a 'costume' and takes a preemptive shot at Troy struggling to eat and drink in cardboard armor — classic Jeff deflection of sincere effort
jokes.explanation: Good Jeff character joke — his costume is 'being handsome,' which is both arrogant and self-aware. The pivot to predicting Troy's functional problems with the costume is a nice double. Character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Note to self: stop watching that movie... the one where they... uh... you know what, never mind.

jokes.text: Shirley's costume announcement: 'Guys, Shirley's costume is once again unwittingly ambiguous. I don't know what she's supposed to be, but she's not Miss Piggy. I repeat, she is not Miss Piggy. You're on your own.'
jokes.setup: Shirley arrives in a costume that is meant to be something specific but reads differently to others
jokes.punchline: Jeff makes a PA-announcement-style disclaimer that she is NOT Miss Piggy — which of course plants the idea that she looks exactly like Miss Piggy — and throws everyone else under the bus to figure it out
jokes.explanation: Jeff's 'announcement' framing is the joke within the joke — the disclaimer format makes it funnier than a direct observation. 'You're on your own' is a perfect abandon. Also plants a callback seed for the later Glinda reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You realize that whole effortless thing is actually really calculated, right? You've probably spent like an hour in front of the mirror perfecting that look of not trying.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not true.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're literally posing right now.

jokes.text: Mystery costume person enters and says 'Hello. Guess who I am.' — long beat — 'Umm. Can't you just say?' / 'No.'
jokes.setup: Someone in an apparently cryptic costume asks people to guess who they are
jokes.punchline: Nobody can guess; the character refuses to just tell them, extending the uncomfortable non-reveal; this recurs throughout the episode
jokes.explanation: Establishes the running gag. The refusal to just say is the joke — a commitment to a bit even as everyone around them gets sick and panics. Works better in the context of the episode's escalating chaos.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're so handsome, it's effortless for you.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, you're so socially awkward, it's effortless for you too.

jokes.text: Pierce sweating and puffy; someone says 'Whoa. Hey, if you get any more sweaty and puffy, your costume's gonna reach authenticity.'
jokes.setup: Pierce is visibly ill — sweating and bloated — in what must be a fat/slovenly costume
jokes.punchline: The sickness is making him look MORE like his costume — dark humor at Pierce's expense that doubles as early foreshadowing of the zombie outbreak
jokes.explanation: Good economy — the joke does two things at once: burns Pierce and plants the idea that something is physically wrong. The 'authenticity' framing is clever.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Shirley, your costume is ambiguous. It could be interpreted as offensive.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: What? What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not saying you look like a [offensive stereotype], because you don't. You absolutely do not look like a [offensive stereotype]. I would never say that. That's not what I'm thinking at all.

jokes.text: Pierce acting delirious; Abed/Troy observe: 'He's acting like the impression of him we do. "What?" "Where am I?" "Where's the black boy in the uniform?"'
jokes.setup: Pierce is behaving erratically due to illness
jokes.punchline: Abed and/or Troy reveal they already have a full impression of Pierce — including a casually racist Pierce quote about 'the black boy in the uniform' — delivered with matter-of-fact affection and horror
jokes.explanation: Sharp character work. The joke is that Pierce's racism is so constant and consistent that the group has fully internalized a spot-on impression, complete with a specific racist quote. The casualness of the delivery makes it land harder. 'The black boy in the uniform' is a character-specific detail that feels entirely true to Pierce.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Pierce, what is wrong with you today?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Nothing! I feel great!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: He's been like this all morning.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Dude, you're being super weird.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm not weird, you guys are weird!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: No, you're definitely being like... *does exaggerated impression* 'I'm Pierce, I'm acting all crazy!'

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: That's not what I sound like!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's exactly what you sound like right now.

jokes.text: Rich checking on Pierce while flirting with Annie: 'Boy, he is just not in very good shape, is he? But you look fantastic. Oh, thank you. Look at you, with your hood.'
jokes.setup: Rich is supposedly doing triage on the very sick Pierce
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots to complimenting Annie mid-diagnosis — clinical detachment replaced by attraction — while Pierce presumably lies there unattended
jokes.explanation: Good cringe comedy — a doctor ignoring a patient to flirt. The specific 'Look at you, with your hood' as the best he can muster is charmingly pathetic. Establishes Rich's character quickly.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I need a doctor!

dialogue.speaker: Rich
dialogue.line: I'm not a doctor.

dialogue.speaker: Rich
dialogue.line: Wait, actually I am a doctor.

jokes.text: Rich after saving Annie from a zombie: 'If that thing comes back, I need one or both of your phone numbers.' Annie: 'Yeah, right.'
jokes.setup: Rich has just heroically saved Annie from a zombie attack
jokes.punchline: He immediately uses the heroism as a flirting opportunity — asking for her number 'just in case' — and she shuts him down flatly
jokes.explanation: Consistent Rich character work. 'One or both' is a funny hedge that implies he's open to group arrangements, which is creepier and funnier than just 'your number.'

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Even as a zombie, I'm still thinking about my money and my stuff.

jokes.text: Jeff to Troy on why his suit works better as a costume than Troy's cardboard robot: 'Well, I'm wearing a $6000 suit, and you spent three days making cardboard robot armor. I'm saying I remind girls less of taking their little brothers to Comic-Con.'
jokes.setup: Troy asks Jeff how he does it with girls at the party despite his minimal costume
jokes.punchline: Jeff's answer is both honestly self-aware (expensive suit) and a precise burn — the Comic-Con little brother image is a vividly specific emasculation
jokes.explanation: The 'taking their little brothers to Comic-Con' image is vivid and specific — it communicates exactly what's wrong with Troy's costume in relation to attraction without being mean-spirited. Good economy and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: How do you do it, man? How do you attract women so easily?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It's simple, Troy. You see a woman you like, you walk up to her, and you tell her exactly what she wants to hear.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's it?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's it. You, on the other hand, walk up to a woman and tell her the truth about yourself, which apparently is a turn-off.

jokes.text: Rich: 'Okay, I'm ruling out food poisoning.' — said definitively after earlier being told NOT to say 'food poisoning' out loud
jokes.setup: Earlier Rich said 'this may be food poisoning' and was told to 'rule it out but not say the words out loud'
jokes.punchline: Rich announces out loud that he's ruling it out — doing exactly the thing he was told not to do, in the exact phrasing he was warned about
jokes.explanation: Clean callback payoff — Rich has the memory of a goldfish, and the specific phrasing ('I'm ruling out food poisoning') technically fulfills the instruction while violating its spirit. Good structural joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh, so girls feel sorry for me? That's sweet. You know what girls feel for you, Troy? Nothing. Absolutely nothing. You're like a computer that learned to talk.

jokes.text: Mystery costume person to Abed: 'Guess who I am.' Abed: 'Michelle Kwan?' 'Wrong.' 'Kristi Yamaguchi?' 'Peggy Fleming.' Abed: 'Just been proven racist by the racist prover.'
jokes.setup: Running gag recurs — mystery person asks Abed to guess their costume
jokes.punchline: Abed guesses two Asian figure skaters before being corrected that it's Peggy Fleming (white); Abed's meta-commentary 'just been proven racist by the racist prover' is both self-aware and deflects blame onto the costume
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The escalating wrong Asian-skater guesses set up Abed's perfect meta-punchline: 'just been proven racist by the racist prover.' The term 'racist prover' is a great neologism — it transfers guilt to the costume/person who constructed the ambiguous situation. Character-perfect for Abed, who would absolutely frame this as a logical system rather than an embarrassment. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, who are you supposed to be?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm an Asian figure skater.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh! Nancy Kerrigan!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oksana Baiul?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: No, I'm a different one.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm doing that thing where I make assumptions based on race. That's... that's not good. I'm being very un-woke right now. I'm being downright... asiophobic.

jokes.text: Mystery costume person approaches Britta: 'Hey, guess who I am.' Britta immediately: 'Drink.'
jokes.setup: Running gag continues; mystery person tries again on a new target
jokes.punchline: Britta refuses to engage and simply uses it as a drinking game prompt — she's already over it
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — Britta's one-word 'Drink' is funnier than any longer response. Character-appropriate for Britta's dismissive 'over it' attitude. The running gag is now paying dividends through variation.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Abed, you can't just wear half the costume! You look ridiculous!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm making a statement about consumer culture and arbitrary matching.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You look like you got dressed in the dark at a Goodwill!

jokes.text: Troy confronts Abed for abandoning their matching costumes: 'But our costumes go together.' Abed: 'I'm just a guy in a spandex suit and a helmet.' / Troy: 'Well, I'm a sexy Dracula. You mean vampire.' / Abed: 'I don't need to know which Dracula I am to be a Dracula. Nerd.'
jokes.setup: Abed has abandoned his half of their matching Halloween costume
jokes.punchline: Abed's correction of 'Dracula' to 'vampire' is the first nerd move; Troy insisting 'I don't need to know which Dracula I am to be a Dracula' and calling Abed a nerd is the ironic reversal — Troy is the one who cares about costumes going together
jokes.explanation: Good Troy/Abed character comedy. The twist is that Troy — the 'cool' one — is the one upset about the matching costume, while Abed plays it off. 'I don't need to know which Dracula I am to be a Dracula' is a great absurdist non-logic. The 'Nerd.' deflection while being objectively the nerdier one is well-calibrated irony.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Dracula is a vampire, Abed. There's no difference.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Dracula is a specific vampire. Not all vampires are Dracula.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Well excuse me for not going to vampire college. Look, I don't need to know all the vampire rules and regulations. I just know Dracula sucks blood and he's dead and he's scary. That's vampire enough for me.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's not about rules, it's about—

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You know what? You're a nerd, Abed. A huge nerd. And I say that with love.

jokes.text: Rich: 'Your symptoms are progressing even faster than everyone else's. How much of that taco meat did you eat?' Alex: 'I didn't eat any. My name is Alex.' Rich: 'Must have transferred through Pierce's bite.'
jokes.setup: Rich asks how much taco meat Alex ate to explain rapid symptom progression
jokes.punchline: Alex corrects that he didn't eat any, then gives his name — implying his name is relevant — and Rich immediately concludes he was bitten by Pierce
jokes.explanation: Functional plot/comedy beat — the name correction mid-diagnosis is a mild comedy of irrelevance. Rich concluding Pierce bit him is darkly funny given Pierce's earlier delirious state.

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: It's Alex. My name is Alex. Why does everyone call me Star-Burns?

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: My parents named me Alex. A-L-E-X. Not Star-Burns.

dialogue.speaker: Star-Burns
dialogue.line: I go by Alex now. Please, just call me Alex.

jokes.text: Annie: 'Annie, you make quite the little nurse.' Rich: 'Thank you, Rich. You're quite a banana.' [uncomfortable pause] 'Jeez, why don't you guys just get a—?'
jokes.setup: Rich compliments Annie on her nursing skills; Annie returns the compliment, referencing Rich's banana costume
jokes.punchline: Jeff's interrupted 'why don't you guys just get a—?' implies he's about to say 'room,' acknowledging the flirtatious tension; the interruption makes it funnier than completing it
jokes.explanation: Jeff's jealous/irritated reaction is the joke — the 'why don't you guys just get a—' is the classic TV shorthand, and cutting it off is funnier than completing it. Character-appropriate for Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Sounds delicious.

jokes.text: Army surplus store owner reads the label: '"Classified Phoenix. If found, repeat key phrase, echo, tango, x-ray, nine, nine, seven."' Dean: 'Yeah, sounds delicious. Anyway...'
jokes.setup: The Dean and store owner investigate the mysterious taco meat container with a classified military label and alphanumeric code
jokes.punchline: The Dean's breezy 'Yeah, sounds delicious. Anyway...' in response to clear evidence of a military biohazard is perfect oblivious optimism
jokes.explanation: Dean's oblivious optimism in the face of obvious danger is perfectly in character. 'Sounds delicious. Anyway' is a great dismissive pivot. The specificity of the military code makes the Dean's breezy reaction funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Leonard, you need to stop this right now or so help me God, I will bake you into a pumpkin pie.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: Is that a threat?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: No, Leonard. It's a promise.

jokes.text: Mystery costume person interrupts chaos to say: 'Okay, one hint. I'm a beloved character from our childhood.'
jokes.setup: Zombie outbreak chaos is escalating; the Army is on the phone
jokes.punchline: Total commitment to the costume bit despite the emergency — giving 'one hint' as if this is still a fun party game
jokes.explanation: The running gag earns its biggest laugh yet by persisting into genuine crisis. The contrast between the emergency and 'okay, one hint' is the entire joke. Good escalation of commitment to the bit.

dialogue.speaker: Rich
dialogue.line: Remember in pottery class when you said—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Rich, there's a crisis happening right now. We can talk about pottery later.

jokes.text: Shirley to zombie Leonard: 'Leonard, behave. I'm a Christian woman. Leonard, you better back that pumpkin ass up or I will make a pie.'
jokes.setup: Leonard (zombie) is apparently getting too close to Shirley in a threatening/inappropriate way
jokes.punchline: Shirley code-switches between Christian propriety and a vivid threat — 'back that pumpkin ass up or I will make a pie' — implying she'll carve him like a jack-o'-lantern
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. Character integration is exceptional — only Shirley could deliver both the Christian propriety opener AND the violent pie threat in the same breath. 'Pumpkin ass' is inspired (Halloween context), and 'I will make a pie' as a threat is brilliantly oblique. The escalation from 'I'm a Christian woman' to graphic vegetable-based violence is perfect. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay everyone, remain calm. We need to evacuate in an orderly fashion. No pushing, no shoving. Single file line to the exits.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: FIRE! EVERYBODY OUT! THERE'S A FIRE! RUN FOR YOUR LIVES!

jokes.text: Rich calls it calmly: 'There's an infection at the party making people act weird and bite each other. We need to coordinate an evacuation without causing unnecessary panic.' Jeff: 'Holy crap, Leonard's a zombie.'
jokes.setup: Rich gives Jeff a measured, clinical briefing about coordinating a calm evacuation
jokes.punchline: Jeff immediately does the opposite — screams 'Holy crap, Leonard's a zombie!' — causing the exact panic Rich warned against
jokes.explanation: Perfect ironic reversal. Rich's calm clinical framing is immediately undercut by Jeff's visceral reaction, which causes the unnecessary panic. Character-specific: Jeff's composure always has a breaking point. The beat between Rich's warning and Jeff's yell is good structure.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Did we just punch a girl in a dinosaur costume?

jokes.text: Jeff screams 'Zombie attack!' — causing mass panic — then immediately: 'Never mind.'
jokes.setup: Jeff causes a stampede with 'Zombie attack!'
jokes.punchline: He immediately recants with 'Never mind' — as if that fixes anything — while chaos presumably continues
jokes.explanation: The 'Never mind' after causing a stampede is a great two-word punchline. Maximum economy. Jeff's breezy non-apology is characteristically him.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: ...and organic free-range butter, non-GMO quinoa, and fair-trade coffee beans...

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: This is a waking nightmare.

jokes.text: Dean quarantining everyone: 'I've been told we need a little baby quarantine until the Army gets here.' 'The Army?' Dean: 'I know, right?' Then: 'They said to wait for six hours. Stay strong.'
jokes.setup: Dean must inform a panicking crowd they're quarantined for six hours until the Army arrives
jokes.punchline: Dean's 'I know, right?' in response to 'The Army?!' is conspiratorial solidarity with the people he's trapping; 'Stay strong' as a send-off is comic inadequacy
jokes.explanation: Dean's 'I know, right?' is a great character beat — he's simultaneously the authority figure and completely out of his depth. The 'Stay strong' is an amusingly feeble pep talk.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're telling me that in 2012, the Mayans predicted the world would end?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's the theory, yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: But it's 2013 and we're all still here. So either the Mayans were wrong, or we're already dead and this is hell.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Troy, that's not how it works.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Nope, I'm convinced. We're zombies. That explains so much about Pierce.

jokes.text: 'Guys, I hate to be the "we've got company" guy, but...' [zombies appear]
jokes.setup: Group is barricaded; zombies are approaching
jokes.punchline: Abed uses the horror movie cliché phrase 'we've got company' — but meta-aware enough to disclaim the role before saying it, then says it anyway
jokes.explanation: Very Abed. The meta-awareness of tropes combined with still using the trope is his entire character. 'I hate to be the "we've got company" guy' is a lovely hedge that acknowledges genre conventions — only Abed would cite the role name before filling it.

dialogue.speaker: Rich
dialogue.line: Your jacket folding technique is terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, well at least I have a jacket. And a technique. Unlike some people whose backgrounds didn't allow for either.

jokes.text: 'You punched a lady bee.'
jokes.setup: During zombie chaos, someone apparently punches a person in a bee costume
jokes.punchline: The observation 'you punched a lady bee' — delivered deadpan — prioritizes costume-accuracy over the violence, as if the gender of the bee costume matters most right now
jokes.explanation: Four words, very funny. The specificity of 'lady bee' (rather than 'woman in a bee costume') is what makes it. The register shift — factual, calm — in the middle of chaos is perfectly executed. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what? You're a kiss-ass.

dialogue.speaker: Rich
dialogue.line: A kiss-ass? That's actually... kind of nice. I like that about myself.

jokes.text: 'Let go of the door, you little bitch.'
jokes.setup: Someone is trying to hold a door closed against zombies
jokes.punchline: The blunt profanity in a network sitcom context — 'you little bitch' directed at presumably a zombie or fellow survivor — is startling and funny for its frankness
jokes.explanation: More of a tonal beat than a crafted joke. The aggression and profanity are funny in context, but it's not particularly constructed comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look, I'll be honest with you. In a real crisis, you're the guy I'd want by my side.

jokes.text: In the middle of zombie chaos and barricading, Jeff asks: 'Last question, and I know it's a long shot. Did anybody shut off the dean's playlist?' — ABBA/voice memos still playing
jokes.setup: Jeff is managing a zombie crisis; the dean's embarrassing iTunes has been playing all episode
jokes.punchline: Jeff's priorities include silencing the dean's playlist even while barricading against zombies — perfectly Jeff, and a callback to the opening iTunes revelation
jokes.explanation: Good callback execution — the playlist has been ambient throughout and Jeff not being able to focus during a zombie apocalypse until the ABBA loop is addressed is funny character work. 'I know it's a long shot' as a hedge is a nice touch.

dialogue.speaker: Rich
dialogue.line: You know what your problem is, Jeff? You don't have any real priorities.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh, that's rich coming from a guy dressed as a banana with a stethoscope. What are you, a doctor's visit to the tropics?

jokes.text: Dean's voice memos continue playing during crisis: 'Two percent milk, eggs, deodorant, Puppy Chow, black light, whole milk... Cotton swabs. It's officially a waking nightmare. Add Eat Pray Love soundtrack to workout mix.'
jokes.setup: The dean's voice memos are still playing while everyone barricades against zombies
jokes.punchline: The grocery list escalates to 'black light' (suspicious), then 'Add Eat Pray Love soundtrack to workout mix' — deeply revealing of the Dean's private self in the worst possible moment
jokes.explanation: Excellent extended callback. The grocery list is mundane then 'black light' raises an eyebrow, and 'Eat Pray Love soundtrack to workout mix' is a perfectly humiliating detail for the Dean. The timing — during a zombie barricade — maximizes the absurdity. 'It's officially a waking nightmare' works both as audience voice and as a reaction to the memos.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: The Army is taking exactly six hours to get here.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's longer than the Oscar ceremony.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, well the Army has standards.

jokes.text: Britta: 'Flavor Flav was right. It's the end of days.' Jeff: 'It can't be the end of days. It's not 2012 yet.' Rich: 'It's not the end of days. It's a rabies-related pathogen...'
jokes.setup: Group panics about the zombie situation
jokes.punchline: Britta invokes Flavor Flav as a prophetic source; Jeff's rebuttal is based on the 2012 Mayan calendar myth (not eschatology); Rich completely deflates both with clinical accuracy
jokes.explanation: Three-person character comedy — Britta's pseudo-intellectual pop-culture prophecy, Jeff's lazy calendar correction, Rich's total deflation with actual science. Each response is character-perfect. Good escalation of absurdity followed by a hard reset.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'd like to thank the Academy for this moment...

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That joke was brought to you by years of therapy and a drinking problem.

jokes.text: 'Flavor Flav was right. It's the end of days.' 'It can't be the end of days. It's not 2012 yet.'
jokes.setup: The group is panicking about the zombie situation as potentially apocalyptic
jokes.punchline: The 2012 end-of-days reference treats the Mayan calendar conspiracy theory as a legitimate calendar-based defense against apocalypse — 'it can't be the end of days yet, the schedule says 2012'
jokes.explanation: The Flavor Flav/end of days combination is absurdist but slightly underbaked. The 2012 joke is period-specific (airing in 2010, before the 2012 Mayan calendar hysteria peak) and reasonably clever — using conspiracy theory logic as genuine comfort. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You need to embrace your inner hero, Troy. Think of Alien. When Ripley faced that xenomorph in her underwear, she didn't back down. She fought.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's not what was happening in that scene.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The point is, vulnerability can be strength.

jokes.text: Jeff to Rich: 'That jacket is worth more than the island you were grown on, Chiquita MD.' Rich: 'Chiquita MD, I like it. This is a good time to let you know I hate you.'
jokes.setup: Jeff insults Rich over something to do with the jacket/barricading situation
jokes.punchline: 'Chiquita MD' as a racial/origin insult is immediately reclaimed by Rich complimenting the nickname ('I like it') before dropping 'this is a good time to let you know I hate you' — formal declaration of hatred delivered cordially
jokes.explanation: Rich's response is the joke — reclaiming an insult as a compliment ('I like it') immediately before formally announcing hatred is funny in its contrasting registers. The timing is sharp. 'Chiquita MD' itself is a good insult portmanteau.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Get away from her, you bitch!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's the line from Aliens.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I know, but I'm a vampire now. I can't say stuff like that.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Why six hours? Are they hosting the Oscars?' Abed: 'And the winner for Best Adapted Oscar Burn: Jeff Winger for Oh, Snap: The Man Who Went There.'
jokes.setup: Jeff makes a sarcastic quip about the Army taking six hours
jokes.punchline: Abed meta-awards Jeff's burn with a formal Oscar announcement — complete with fabricated film title 'Oh, Snap: The Man Who Went There' — treating Jeff's everyday snark as award-worthy cinema
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. Abed's hyper-specific Oscar announcement format — including the fabricated title 'Oh, Snap: The Man Who Went There' — is inspired. The joke is simultaneously meta (Abed frames reality as film), character-specific (only Abed would do this), and contains a genuinely good fake movie title that escalates the comedy. 'Best Adapted Oscar Burn' as a category is perfect absurdist specificity. One of the episode's highest-craft moments.

dialogue.speaker: Rich
dialogue.line: I'm fine, I'm totally fine. Just a little cough, maybe a slight fever, but nothing serious.

dialogue.speaker: Rich
dialogue.line: Been like this for... what, three weeks now? Four? But I'm handling it great.

jokes.text: Rich: 'Those people don't have six hours. In three hours, they're gonna suffer brain damage. After that, they're gonna be dead.' Jeff: 'Do something for the zombies?'
jokes.setup: Rich argues they need to help the infected people outside
jokes.punchline: Jeff's incredulous 'Do something for the zombies?' frames the infected as monsters rather than sick classmates — characteristically selfish framing played for laughs
jokes.explanation: Jeff's self-preservation logic played as comedy. Functional character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know, Rich, I have to say, even infected and falling apart, you're still somehow less annoying than you usually are.

jokes.text: Troy refuses to go on the thermostat mission: 'I'm not Ripley, Abed. I'm a cool, sexy Dracula. I make love to ladies and I survive.' Rich: 'I'm with Troy.'
jokes.setup: Abed invokes Alien's Ripley to motivate Troy to go fix the thermostat through zombie territory
jokes.punchline: Troy rejects the action hero identity and substitutes his own — 'cool, sexy Dracula who makes love to ladies' — as a competing survival philosophy; Rich immediately endorsing it is perfect
jokes.explanation: Troy's alternative self-image — 'I make love to ladies and I survive' — is a genuinely funny articulation of cowardice dressed up as philosophy. Rich's immediate 'I'm with Troy' adds a perfect button. Character-specific for Troy's bravado-over-action persona.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Wait, these aren't zombies, they're just people in grey makeup!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: That's not even a zombie costume, that's just... that's just Kevin from accounting!

jokes.text: Annie: 'The banana said so.' [referring to Rich's medical expertise]
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to convince everyone to trust Rich's medical assessment
jokes.punchline: She refers to him as 'the banana' because of his costume — treating his expert authority as inseparable from his humiliating outfit
jokes.explanation: Quick absurdist beat — 'the banana said so' as a credentialing phrase is funny precisely because it both invokes and undermines authority. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I'm going to die as Miss Piggy.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You're not Miss Piggy. You're a big fat pig.

jokes.text: Rich reveals he's been bitten: 'I felt like maybe I was special.' Jeff: 'Special? You're not special. I'm special. I was bit 10 minutes ago and I'm f—' [immediately turns zombie]
jokes.setup: Rich confesses he was bitten and thought he might have immunity
jokes.punchline: Jeff interrupts to claim HE is the special one with immunity — then immediately zombie-turns mid-sentence, undercutting his claim completely
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a highlight of Jeff characterization. The setup is Rich's (relatable) hope that he might be special/immune. Jeff's narcissistic interruption to claim HE is the special one is perfectly in character. The cut-off mid-boast — 'I was bit 10 minutes ago and I'm f—' — with an immediate turn is structurally perfect. The joke works on multiple levels: deflates Rich, deflates Jeff, and pays off with physical comedy. 'Oh, great. Nobody's special!' as the response button is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Jeff, before I go... you're not a racist. You're just... you're just an idiot.

jokes.text: 'Oh, great. Nobody's special!'
jokes.setup: Both Rich and Jeff are now confirmed bitten/turned
jokes.punchline: Annie's frustrated realization that neither of the two hopeful 'special' cases worked out is delivered as a small despair at the concept of specialness rather than the zombie apocalypse
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the previous joke. 'Nobody's special' could be a profound statement about humanity but here it's about zombie immunity. The phrasing is economic and delivers a different comedic punch than the setup joke.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: So let me get this straight. We're in an abandoned mansion, it's midnight, and we just split up. What could possibly go wrong? Oh wait, I know this one from every horror movie ever made. We're all gonna die. Specifically, me first, because I'm the funny one, and apparently that's a death sentence in these situations.

jokes.text: Annie tells zombie Rich: 'Hey, Rich, just so you know, I hate you less now. That's how much I hate your normal self.'
jokes.setup: Rich has turned into a zombie; Annie addresses him
jokes.punchline: Annie's zombie-Rich confession — she hates him less as a zombie — is both a declaration of how annoying he was while flirting AND a callback to Rich's earlier 'this is a good time to let you know I hate you' pattern
jokes.explanation: Sharp character moment. The logic — she hates zombie-Rich LESS because his flirting has stopped — is both funny and slightly poignant. Mirrors Rich's earlier formal hatred declaration.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're saying that friendship and commitment make you a nerd?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: No, that's not what I'm saying.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Because I'm pretty sure those are the things that make someone NOT a nerd.

jokes.text: During zombie chase in basement: 'Hamster! A hamster! Way to go. Run, run!'
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed are fleeing through the basement
jokes.punchline: They encounter a hamster in the basement — a completely unexpected element — and celebrate it despite being chased by zombies
jokes.explanation: Random-absurdist beat — the hamster is inexplicable but Troy and Abed's delight at it mid-crisis is a good character beat. Somewhat undercut by the 'random = funny' trap.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm not a nerd! And I'm not even going to dignify this conversation with a response.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's right, I'm staying out of this.

jokes.text: Shirley: 'Oh, this is how I die, as Miss Piggy.' Jeff: 'You're not Miss Piggy. You're Glinda the Good Witch.'
jokes.setup: Shirley despairs that she'll die in an ambiguous costume everyone thought was Miss Piggy
jokes.punchline: Jeff finally names the costume correctly — Glinda the Good Witch — which both vindicates Shirley and reveals Jeff knew all along
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff. The fact that Jeff knew all along (and even made the disclaimer 'she's NOT Miss Piggy') but waited until a near-death moment to tell her is a perfect character reveal. The callback structure is elegant — the earlier setup ('not Miss Piggy') pays off here with the correct answer. Shirley's despair at dying 'as Miss Piggy' is also perfectly funny.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You know what I think? I think someone's throwing the same cat down here over and over again.

jokes.text: Shirley: 'You knew?' Jeff: [doesn't answer, then] 'Just so you know, I've always loved Peggy Fleming.' [to mystery costume person]
jokes.setup: Shirley asks if Jeff knew her costume all along; Jeff pivots to complimenting the mystery person on their Peggy Fleming costume
jokes.punchline: Jeff evades answering Shirley and uses the moment to pay a compliment to the mystery costume person — also a callback to the racist prover moment
jokes.explanation: Jeff's evasion by pivoting to compliment the Peggy Fleming costume is a triple-callback payoff: confirms the mystery costume, resolves Jeff's 'I always knew' character detail, and ties back to the racist prover gag. Good structural density.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm done being a hero. I'm like a soup that's been left out on the counter. At first, I'm hot and everyone wants me. But the longer I sit there, the more I turn into a weird, crusty, room-temperature disappointment that nobody wants to touch.

jokes.text: Abed drily: 'Oh, cool. A dark basement. I was just thinking we should be doing this in a dark basement.'
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed arrive in a dark basement while fleeing zombies
jokes.punchline: Abed's deadpan 'I was just thinking we should be doing this in a dark basement' — the horror movie trope of characters inexplicably going somewhere dark and dangerous — frames his own situation as clichéd
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed meta-commentary on horror conventions — delivered while living through them. 'I was just thinking we should be doing this in a dark basement' is irony that works as both genre criticism and character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No, no, no! This is a Tom Ford suit!

jokes.text: Troy confronts Abed about the costume: 'Troy, why did you ditch your costume?' / 'Why bring that up now, Abed? We might die down here.' / 'All the more reason to get this ironed out. You called me a nerd. What defines a nerd? Committing to a costume with your best friend, is that what nerds do?'
jokes.setup: They're in a dark basement hiding from zombies
jokes.punchline: Abed uses the near-death situation as leverage to have a conversation about the costume slight — 'all the more reason to get this ironed out' — his logic being that if they die, it'll be unresolved
jokes.explanation: Excellent Abed character work. His insistence on resolving the costume dispute while hiding from zombies — 'all the more reason to get this ironed out' — is perfectly Abed: logical to him, absurd to everyone else. 'What defines a nerd? Committing to a costume with your best friend, is that what nerds do?' as his defensive logic is both funny and character-illuminating. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: In horror movies, the black guy always dies first. I'm not black, but I'm going to die anyway because I'm expendable. It's like I'm the black guy of white guys.

jokes.text: They're startled by a noise — 'It was just a cat. Let's keep moving.' — then immediately: 'Holy crap. What is up with that cat? Is someone throwing it? Let's keep moving.' / 'Let's not keep moving, because there is an insane cat down here.'
jokes.setup: Noise in the basement turns out to be a cat — relief — then the cat is apparently terrifying
jokes.punchline: Troy insists on addressing the insane cat rather than the zombies — escalating threat displacement: zombies (accepted) → insane cat (unacceptable)
jokes.explanation: Good escalation joke — the relief of 'just a cat' is immediately replaced by a different terror. Troy's insistence that the cat is the more pressing problem ('back burner, Troy. This cat has to be dealt with') inverts the threat hierarchy hilariously. 'Is someone throwing it?' is a great specific detail.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I know.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I know you know. I've always known.

jokes.text: Abed: 'But what about the zombies?' Troy: 'Back burner, Troy. This cat has to be dealt with.'
jokes.setup: Abed wants to continue the thermostat mission past the terrifying cat
jokes.punchline: Troy tells Abed to put zombies 'on the back burner' because the cat is the priority — complete inversion of threat logic
jokes.explanation: 'Back burner, Troy' — Troy telling Abed to put zombies on the back burner by using his own name as an instruction — is a great compressed joke. The cat beats zombies in Troy's risk assessment, which is absurd and character-perfect (Troy's fears often don't match reality's threat level).

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, I'm realizing something. To be a hero, I have to do nerdy things like study maps, learn logistics, understand complex plans...

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh no. Oh no no no. Being a hero means being a nerd.

jokes.text: Jeff's refusal to go through the window/fence: 'He doesn't wanna dirty his suit. For real?' / 'Clothes make the man, Troy.'
jokes.setup: Three options for escape — Troy advocates a window that requires climbing; Jeff refuses
jokes.punchline: Jeff won't dirty his $6000 suit to escape zombies; his justification ('clothes make the man') is sincere and completely misapplied
jokes.explanation: Jeff's vanity during a zombie escape is consistent with his character. 'Clothes make the man' as a sincere justification for not saving your life is good character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Hey zombies, you just got... Troy'd!

jokes.text: Jeff's jacket getting stretched as he goes through the window: 'That's my jacket. My jacket, you're stretching it! You're stretching it!'
jokes.setup: Jeff is being pulled through a window/fence in his expensive suit
jokes.punchline: Jeff's primary concern — screamed repeatedly — is the jacket stretching, not the zombie threat
jokes.explanation: Physical payoff on the suit vanity joke. The repeated 'you're stretching it!' is funny in its escalation but the joke is essentially the same character beat repeated.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: This is it! Time to take them down! Come on!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait — this isn't working! Why won't they stay down?!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's not fair! They're not following the rules! Zombies aren't supposed to be this coordinated!

jokes.text: Abed to Troy: 'Troy, make me proud. Be the first black man to make it to the end.'
jokes.setup: Abed is sacrificing himself so Troy can make it to safety
jokes.punchline: Abed frames Troy's survival as a horror movie trope subversion — 'be the first black man to make it to the end' — an explicit meta-commentary on the genre's racist survival statistics
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best and most memorable jokes. Abed's self-sacrifice is framed entirely through horror movie genre literacy — specifically the well-documented trope of Black characters dying first. The joke works on multiple levels: it's funny as meta-commentary, it's character-perfect for Abed, it honors the trope while subverting it, and it has emotional stakes (Abed is genuinely sacrificing himself here). 'Make me proud' adds a surprisingly moving dimension. Near-perfect character integration — only Abed would say this. Highly quotable, definitely a standout.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Annie, you're like Sleeping Beauty, except you're a zombie!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: And I'm Captain Kirk, and this is my Prime Directive: to boldly go... away from you!

jokes.text: Abed to Troy: 'I love you.' Troy: 'I know.'
jokes.setup: Abed is sacrificing himself at the gate as zombies close in
jokes.punchline: 'I love you / I know' is a direct Star Wars callback (Han Solo/Princess Leia) — Abed frames his own emotional sacrifice through film reference, which both earns a laugh and is genuinely moving
jokes.explanation: The episode's peak moment. This joke is exceptional because it functions simultaneously as comedy AND genuine emotion. The Star Wars reference ('I know' as the Solo response) is perfect character integration for Abed, who would absolutely speak in movie quotes at the most sincere moment of his life. But it also genuinely works as an emotional beat — it IS a love confession, filtered through Abed's cinematic brain. The economy is perfect (four words total). The audience simultaneously laughs and feels something. This is craft-forward Community at its best.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Hey, congratulations you guys. You got me. You're very fast. You're very... bitey.

jokes.text: Troy confronts the Dean outside: 'Give me the keys. People are gonna get brain damage if someone doesn't help.' Dean temporizes: 'Troy, there is something called chain of command, so unfortunately...' Troy walks away. Dean: 'No. Are you crazy? How are you gonna survive those zombies?' Troy: 'I'm gonna be a nerd.'
jokes.setup: Troy needs the keys to get back in and fix the thermostat; the Dean tries to invoke authority
jokes.punchline: Troy's declaration 'I'm gonna be a nerd' — accepting Abed's framing of nerds as the heroes who commit — is the callback payoff to the Troy/Abed costume argument; it's his character arc summarized in four words
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. 'I'm gonna be a nerd' reclaims the insult as the episode's hero move — nerds are the ones who commit to costumes, to friends, to saving everyone. It's funny and emotionally resonant as a character arc beat. The Dean's 'Better have a plan B' follows, which is appropriately deflating. High marks for structure and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Even as a zombie, Jeff's still got that cool guy thing going on.

jokes.text: Troy walks back into zombie territory with the LARP-ish fantasy approach: 'That's right. Prepare to meet the power of imagination.' — then immediately: 'Okay, I don't know why I thought this would work.'
jokes.setup: Troy declares he's going to use 'the power of imagination' to fight his way through zombies
jokes.punchline: He immediately deflates his own heroic declaration — 'I don't know why I thought this would work' — before it even has a chance to fail
jokes.explanation: Good self-deflationary joke — Troy's heroic declaration collapses before it even starts. The speed of the reversal is what makes it work.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Six hours. That's an oddly specific response time.

dialogue.speaker: Military Officer
dialogue.line: Well, we've found that's how long it takes for the flesh to stop moving.

jokes.text: Troy fighting zombie Annie: 'Hello, zombie Annie. What big fists you have, in your face.'
jokes.setup: Troy encounters zombie Annie during his mission
jokes.punchline: Troy riffs on 'What big eyes you have' (Little Red Riding Hood) but improvises 'What big fists you have' mid-punch — the fairy tale register while punching a friend is delightfully incongruous
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist riff — 'what big fists you have' adapts the fairy tale template to describe the threat, and 'in your face' as both idiom and literal action is a small wordplay win.

dialogue.speaker: Military Officer
dialogue.line: We've discovered survivors. What should we do about them?

dialogue.speaker: Military Officer
dialogue.line: You know what, let's just drug them and wipe their memories.

jokes.text: Troy fighting zombie Magnitude: 'Beam this up, Scotty. In your face.'
jokes.setup: Troy encounters zombie Magnitude (whose catchphrase is 'Pop pop!')
jokes.punchline: Troy misquotes Star Trek ('Beam me up, Scotty' → 'Beam this up, Scotty') while punching — the wrong reference mixed with action hero talk
jokes.explanation: Minor joke — the misquote is functional but not particularly inspired. It's one of a series of similar beats and the least strong of them.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Wait, so someone drugged the punch bowl? And it wasn't me?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I've been trying to do that for years.

jokes.text: Troy finds zombie Shirley: 'Zombie Shirley. I don't know what you are, but in your face!'
jokes.setup: Troy encounters yet another zombie friend
jokes.punchline: The callback to Shirley's ambiguous costume — 'I don't know what you are' — even in a fight scene, is the joke; and the perfunctory 'in your face!' continues the running action-hero talk
jokes.explanation: Good callback — 'I don't know what you are' resurfaces the costume ambiguity at an absurd moment. The fact that Troy can't identify Shirley's costume even now gets a deserved laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What about that zombie movie?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: No way. After what we went through, I'm done with zombies.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Come on, it's a classic!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Troy, we literally fought the undead. I'm not watching people pretend to do it for entertainment.

jokes.text: Britta gets bitten: 'Okay, okay. I've been bit, y'all.' Jeff (zombie): 'Damn. Congrats. You did what zombies do.'
jokes.setup: Britta is bitten by a zombie
jokes.punchline: Jeff — now a zombie — still has enough coherence to condescendingly congratulate the zombie ('Congrats. You did what zombies do.') — Jeff's superiority complex persists into zombification
jokes.explanation: One of the funnier Jeff jokes in the episode. 'Congrats. You did what zombies do.' — delivered by a zombie Jeff to another zombie about basic zombie behavior — is a perfect expression of Jeff's condescension surviving zombification. Character integration is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: George Takei
dialogue.line: Hello, I'm George Takei, and I'm offering a free voicemail message for anyone named Kevin. When they call, they'll hear me say: 'Kevin, this is Captain Kirk. We need you on the bridge immediately. The dilithium crystals are failing, and you're the only one who can save the ship.'

jokes.text: Shot of zombie Jeff — the camera lingers — someone observes: 'Still cool as a zombie.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is now a zombie
jokes.punchline: Even zombified, Jeff apparently looks cool — the show acknowledges the unfair reality that Jeff is attractive even in a degraded state
jokes.explanation: Good callback to Jeff's 'accidentally handsome' costume. The observation 'still cool as a zombie' is a funny note on Jeff's indefensible attractiveness even in a worst-case scenario.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Tell Shirley... tell her I always loved her. We had a moment together once. A beautiful moment.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: What? We did NOT!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: She'll never know the truth.

jokes.text: Army arrives exactly on time: 'Wow, six hours on the dot.' 'Yeah, well, practice makes perfect.'
jokes.setup: The army arrives at the promised six-hour mark
jokes.punchline: 'Practice makes perfect' — the casual admission that the military has done this before, and that punctuality on zombie quarantines has been refined through repetition, implies a disturbing history
jokes.explanation: 'Practice makes perfect' in the context of military zombie containment is a quietly excellent dark joke — the matter-of-fact implication of prior incidents. The casualness of the delivery makes it funnier than any explicit elaboration would.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Troy, it's me. I'm calling to tell you that Shirley and I hooked up.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Why would you call me to tell me that? Why would you do that?

jokes.text: Army officer: 'Going in.' Dean: 'Dose what now?'
jokes.setup: Officer says 'dose these suckers' and moves to execute
jokes.punchline: Dean's delayed 'Dose what now?' — processing the information too slowly — is a perfect character reaction beat
jokes.explanation: Quick reaction beat — the Dean processing one beat behind. Good economy, functions as a grace note after the previous joke.

jokes.text: Post-treatment, everyone has amnesia: 'You remember nothing past your decision to be Lady Gaga?' Dean looks relieved/horrified.
jokes.setup: Everyone's been dosed and has no memory of the zombie party
jokes.punchline: The Army's dose conveniently erases all memory — the Dean's last clean memory is his Lady Gaga costume decision, which is both his greatest shame and greatest pride
jokes.explanation: Good callback — the last clean memory being the Lady Gaga costume is both a tidy reset and a commentary on the Dean's self-regard. 'Past your decision to be Lady Gaga' is a funny specific phrase.

jokes.text: 'I can't believe that somebody would mass-roofie an entire party.' Jeff: 'I can't believe it wasn't me.' Britta: 'I can't believe I believe you.' Jeff: 'And I don't.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is processing that the Army dosed the party without consent
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'I can't believe it wasn't me' implies he would mass-roofie a party if he thought of it; Britta believes him (revealing her low opinion of him); Jeff then denies it, in the wrong order (the denial coming after she said she believed him)
jokes.explanation: Excellent rapid-fire three-part exchange. The structure is sharp: (1) Jeff confesses he would have done it, (2) Britta believes it readily, (3) Jeff denies it only after she accepts it — the reversal of normal social order (deny first, have believed later) is funny. Character integration is high — this is very Jeff and very Britta.

jokes.text: Troy and Abed's movie selection: 'Aliens, cyborgs or zombies?' Troy: 'I don't know why, but I'm kind of over zombies.' Abed: 'Yeah, I don't feel like anything action-heavy. How about something light? You seen Marmaduke?'
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed are picking a movie to watch after surviving a zombie attack they don't remember
jokes.punchline: Troy is 'kind of over zombies' for reasons he can't articulate (the erased memory); the contrast of surviving a zombie attack and then choosing Marmaduke as the 'light' alternative is perfect
jokes.explanation: Good ironic closing beat — the memory wipe means they're unconsciously avoiding the genre that traumatized them. 'I'm kind of over zombies' as a profound-without-knowing-why statement is clever. Marmaduke as the light alternative is a great specific choice for its lowbrow incongruity.

jokes.text: George Takei narrates the ending: 'And so Troy and Abed went back to the dormitory for a viewing of Marmaduke. I'm George Takei.'
jokes.setup: Takei bookends the episode with the same gravitas he opened with
jokes.punchline: The portentous narration is applied to the mundane event of watching Marmaduke — the same tonal mismatch as the opening, now paid off with specific content
jokes.explanation: Good bookend — Takei narrating the mundane as epic is the structural joke of the episode's framing device. 'A viewing of Marmaduke' as the climax of Takei's narration is a good deflation.

jokes.text: George Takei: 'And if your name is Kevin, here's a little freebie for your cell phone. Hi, Kevin can't come to the phone. He's on a spaceship with me, George Takei. Please leave a message. You're welcome, Kevins. Happy Halloween.'
jokes.setup: Takei wraps up the episode narration
jokes.punchline: He offers a free voicemail message specifically for people named Kevin — a completely unprompted, oddly specific gift that reveals a generous but bizarre Takei persona
jokes.explanation: Genuinely funny and unexpected post-credits beat. 'You're welcome, Kevins' — the plural — implies Takei has thought this through and is addressing all Kevins as a constituency. The specificity of Kevin (not 'everyone') is what makes it absurdly funny. 'He's on a spaceship with me, George Takei' is a great sentence.

jokes.text: Chang's voicemail to Troy: 'Troy, this is Chang. There's not much time. I don't think we're gonna make it. Listen, if you survive, please spread this message for me: Shirley and I totally did it.' / [Shirley in background]: 'Chang, what are you doing?' / Chang: 'Nothing. Gotta go.' / Troy: 'Why did he call me?'
jokes.setup: Dramatic voicemail setup: 'there's not much time, I don't think we're gonna make it, if you survive spread this message'
jokes.punchline: The 'important message' is that Chang slept with Shirley — not survival information — delivered in full dying-hero register; Shirley's horrified 'what are you doing?' from the background, Chang's guilty 'nothing, gotta go'; Troy's baffled 'why did he call me?' as the button
jokes.explanation: Excellent closing joke — probably the episode's most structurally complete bit. The setup mimics heroic last-transmission tropes perfectly ('there's not much time,' 'if you survive'). The misdirection is total — this sounds like vital survival information. The punchline deflates everything: it's gossip. Shirley's background protest and Chang's immediate guilt ('nothing, gotta go') are perfect. Troy's 'why did he call me?' — not 'why would he say that' but 'why ME' — is the ideal button, suggesting this call was both wrong in content and recipient. High structure marks, highly quotable, great closing note.
